*Saṃsāra* (in Sanskrit (संसार) and Pali) in Buddhism <https://
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism> is the beginningless cycle of repeated
birth <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebirth_(Buddhism)>, mundane
existence and dying again.^[1] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTETrainor200458,_'''Quote:'''_"Buddhism_shares_with_Hinduism_the_doctrine_of_Samsara,_whereby_all_beings_pass_through_an_unceasing_cycle_of_birth,_death_and_rebirth_until_they_find_a_means_of_liberation_from_the_cycle._However,_Buddhism_differs_from_Hinduism_in_rejecting_the_assertion_that_every_human_being_possesses_a_changeless_[[soul]]_which_constitutes_their_ultimate_identity,_and_which_transmigrates_from_one_incarnation_to_the_next.-1> Samsara is considered to be suffering (Skt. /duḥkha <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Du%E1%B8%A5kha>/; P. /dukkha/), or generally unsatisfactory and painful.^[2] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2010-2> It is perpetuated by desire and ignorance (Skt. /avidyā <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avidy%C4%81_(Buddhism)>;/ P. /avijjā/), and the resulting karma and sensuousness.^[3] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJuergensmeyerRoof2011271-272-3> ^[4] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcClelland2010172,_240-4> ^[5] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamsTribeWynne201218–19,_chapter_1-5>

Rebirths occur in six realms of existence, namely three good realms
(heavenly <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deva_(Buddhism)>, demi-god
<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asura_(Buddhism)>, human) and three evil
realms (animal, ghosts <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preta>, hell
<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naraka_(Buddhism)>).^[note 1]
<#cite_note-realms2-7> Saṃsāra ends when a being attains nirvāṇa
<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nirvana_(Buddhism)>, which is the
extinction of desire and acquisition of true insight into the nature of
reality as impermanent <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anicca> and non-
self <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatta>.^[7] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEBuswellGimello19927–8,_83–84-8> ^[8] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEChoong199928–
29,_Quote:_"Seeing_(''passati'')_the_nature_of_things_as_impermanent_leads_to_the_removal_of_the_view_of_self,_and_so_to_the_realisation_of_nirvana."-9> ^[9] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTERahula201451-58-10> ^[note 2] <#cite_note-nirvanakc-11>


Characteristics

[edit <https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?
title=Sa%E1%B9%83s%C4%81ra_(Buddhism)&action=edit&section=1>]

In Buddhism, /saṃsāra/ is the beginningless and endless cycle of life,
death, and rebirth characterized by suffering.^[2] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEWilson2010-2> ^[10] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTELaumakis200897-12>
Passages from the Samyutta Nikaya <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Samyutta_Nikaya> propose that this process is beginningless, fueled by
the ignorance and craving of beings.^[11] <#cite_note-13> This unending
transmigration across the six realms (Skt. /gati/, lit. "paths")^[12]
<#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowker1997-14> lacks a particular direction or
purpose.^[13] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGethin1998119-15> ^[14] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEAjahn_Sucitto201037–38-16> ^[note 3] <#cite_note-realms-18>
Samsara is characterized by suffering (Skt. /duḥkha <https://
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Du%E1%B8%A5kha>/; P. /dukkha <https://
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dukkha>/),^[note 4] <#cite_note-20> and relates to
the Four Noble Truths <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Noble_Truths>
in Buddhism, as dukkha <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dukkha> is the
essence of Samsara.^[17] <#cite_note-21> ^[18] <#cite_note-22> Every
rebirth is temporary and impermanent. In each rebirth one is born and
dies, to be reborn elsewhere in accordance with one's own karma.^[19]
<#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliams200274–75-23> It is perpetuated by one's
ignorance (Skt. and P. /avidyā <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Avidy%C4%81_(Buddhism)>/), particularly ignorance regarding impermanence
(Skt. /anityā <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anitya>/; P. /anicca
<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anicca>/) and no-self (Skt. /anātman
<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An%C4%81tman>/; P. /anatta <https://
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatta>/),^[20] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEKeown200481,_281-24> ^[21] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowler199939–
42-25> which leads to craving.^[note 5] <#cite_note-
Ignorance_and_craving-28> Samsara continues until liberation is attained
by means of insight and nirvana <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Nirvana_(Buddhism)>,^[15] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEKeown2000Kindle_locations_702-706-17> ^[note 2] <#cite_note-
nirvanakc-11> the extinguishment of desires and the gaining of true
insight into impermanence <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anicca> and
non-self <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatta> reality.^[7]
<#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuswellGimello19927–8,_83–84-8> ^[8] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEChoong199928–
29,_Quote:_"Seeing_(''passati'')_the_nature_of_things_as_impermanent_leads_to_the_removal_of_the_view_of_self,_and_so_to_the_realisation_of_nirvana."-9> ^[9] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTERahula201451-58-10> Outside of a Buddhist context, similar notions of cyclic existence date back to 800 BCE.^[25] <#cite_note-31>


Mechanism

[edit <https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?
title=Sa%E1%B9%83s%C4%81ra_(Buddhism)&action=edit&section=2>]

Saṃsāra in Buddhism asserts that there is no permanently unchanging
entity that undergoes the endless cycles of rebirth, and this
distinguishes it from the Hindu <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism>
and Jain <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jainism> views of saṃsāra.^[26]
<#cite_note-
FOOTNOTETrainor200458,_Quote:_"Buddhism_shares_with_Hinduism_the_doctrine_of_Samsara,_whereby_all_beings_pass_through_an_unceasing_cycle_of_birth,_death_and_rebirth_until_they_find_a_means_of_liberation_from_the_cycle._However,_Buddhism_differs_from_Hinduism_in_rejecting_the_assertion_that_every_human_being_possesses_a_changeless_soul_which_constitutes_their_ultimate_identity,_and_which_transmigrates_from_one_incarnation_to_the_next.-32> ^[27] <#cite_note-naomiappleton76-33> This is known as no-self <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-self> (Skt. /anātman/; P. /anatta/).^[28] <#cite_note-britannicaanatta-34> ^[29] <#cite_note-anatta3sources-35>

Early Buddhist texts suggest that the Buddha faced a difficulty in
explaining what is reborn and how rebirth occurs, after he invented the
concept that there is "no self."^[30] <#cite_note-Kalupahana1975p115-36>
Later Buddhist scholars, such as the fifth-century Pali scholar-monk
Buddhaghosa <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhaghosa>, suggested that
the lack of a self or soul does not mean lack of continuity; and the
rebirth across different realms of birth – such as heavenly, human,
animal, hellish and others – occurs in the same way that a flame is
transferred from one candle to another.^[31] <#cite_note-37> ^[32]
<#cite_note-38> Buddhaghosa attempted to explain rebirth mechanism with
"rebirth-linking consciousness" (/patisandhi/).^[33] <#cite_note-39>
^[34] <#cite_note-Doniger1980p168-40>

Buddhist traditions diverge in their understanding of the exact process
of rebirth. The Early Buddhist Schools <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Early_Buddhist_schools> were divided on whether or not there existed an
intermediate state (Skt. /antarābhava/ <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Antarabh%C4%81va>) between lives.^[35] <#cite_note-41> These doctrinal
camps filtered into contemporary Buddhism with conservative Theravada
Buddhists asserting that rebirth is immediate while the Mahāyāna schools
generally agree that there is an intermediate state of up to forty-nine
days before the being is reborn.^[36] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEBuswellLopez201349–50,_708–709-42> ^[37] <#cite_note-43> ^[38]
<#cite_note-44>

In the framework of the Two Truths <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Two_truths_doctrine> as capitulated by the third-century Mahayanist
scholar-monk Nagarjuna <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagarjuna>,
saṃsāra and nirvāṇa <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nirvana_(Buddhism)>
are identical in the ultimate truth.^[39] <#cite_note-45>

Buddhist cosmology typically identifies six realms of rebirth and
existence: gods, demi-gods, humans, animals, hungry ghosts and
hells.^[40] <#cite_note-46> Earlier Buddhist texts refer to five realms
rather than six realms; when described as five realms, the god realm and
demi-god realm constitute a single realm.^[6] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEBuswell2004711-712-6>

The six realms are typically divided into three higher realms (good,
fortunate) and three lower realms (evil, unfortunate), with all realms
of rebirth being Independent completely of reality and nature in all
forms, with the deva realm being the "ultimate" reality.^[41]
<#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcClelland201040,_107-47> ^[42] <#cite_note-48> The
three higher realms are the realms of the gods, humans and demi-gods;
the three lower realms are the realms of the animals, hungry ghosts and
hell beings.^[43] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDalai_Lama19925–8-49> ^[44]
<#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatrul_Rinpoche199861–99-50> The six realms are
organized into thirty-one levels <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty-
One_Planes_of_Existence> in East Asian literature.^[45] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEKeown201335–40-51> Buddhist texts describe these realms as
follows:^[43] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDalai_Lama19925–8-49> ^[44]
<#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatrul_Rinpoche199861–99-50>

  * *God realm (deva <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
    Deva_(Buddhism)>):*^[46] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrainor200462-52> ^[47]
    <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcClelland2010136-53> the realm of the gods is
    the most pleasant among the six realms, and can be subdivided into
    many planes of existence.^[48] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeown201335-54> A
    rebirth in this heavenly realm stems from accumulating wholesome
    karma.^[46] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrainor200462-52> A deva does not
    need to work, and is able to enjoy in the heavenly realm all
    pleasures found on earth. However, the pleasures of this realm lead
    to attachment (/Upādāna <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
    Up%C4%81d%C4%81na>/), lack of spiritual pursuits and therefore no
    nirvana.^[49] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeown201337-55> The vast majority
    of Buddhist lay people have historically pursued Buddhist rituals
    and practices motivated with rebirth into deva realm.^[46]
    <#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrainor200462-52> ^[note 6] <#cite_note-58> The
    deva realm in Buddhist practice in Southeast and East Asia include
    gods found in Hindu traditions such as Indra <https://
    en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indra> and Brahma <https://en.wikipedia.org/
    wiki/Brahma>, and concepts in Hindu cosmology such as Mount Meru
    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Meru>.^[52] <#cite_note-
    FOOTNOTEKeown201337–38-59>
  * *Human realm (/manuṣya <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
    Human_beings_in_Buddhism>/):*^[46] <#cite_note-
    FOOTNOTETrainor200462-52> ^[47] <#cite_note-
    FOOTNOTEMcClelland2010136-53> Buddhism asserts that one is reborn in
    this realm with vastly different physical endowments and moral
    natures because of a being's past karma.^[53] <#cite_note-60> A
    rebirth in this realm is considered as fortunate because it offers
    an opportunity to attain nirvana and end the Saṃsāra cycle.^[46]
    <#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrainor200462-52> ^[54] <#cite_note-
    FOOTNOTEKeown201336–37-61>
  * *Demi-god realm (asuras <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
    Asura_(Buddhism)>):*^[46] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrainor200462-52>
    ^[47] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcClelland2010136-53> the third realm of
    existence in Buddhism. Demi-gods are notable for their anger and
    some supernatural powers. They fight with the gods, or trouble the
    humans through illnesses and natural disasters.^[46] <#cite_note-
    FOOTNOTETrainor200462-52> They accumulate karma, and are reborn.
  * *Animal realm (tiryag <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
    Animals_in_Buddhism>):*^[55] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrainor200463-62>
    is the state of existence of a being as an animal.^[47] <#cite_note-
    FOOTNOTEMcClelland2010136-53> This realm is traditionally thought to
    be similar to a hellish realm, because animals are believed in
    Buddhist texts to be driven by impulse and instinct, they prey on
    each other and suffer.^[56] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeown201336-63> Some
    Buddhist texts assert that plants belong to this realm, with
    primitive consciousness.^[55] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrainor200463-62> 

<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
File:Hungry_Ghosts_Scroll_Kyoto_5.jpg>Hungry ghosts in a 12th-century
painting from Kyoto, Japan

  * *Hungry ghost realm:*^[46] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrainor200462-52>
    hungry ghosts and other restless spirits (preta <https://
    en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preta>)^[47] <#cite_note-
    FOOTNOTEMcClelland2010136-53> are rebirths caused by karma of
    excessive craving and attachments. They do not have a body, are
    invisible and constitute only "subtle matter" of a being. Buddhist
    texts describe them as beings who are extremely thirsty and hungry,
    with very small mouths but very large stomachs.^[56] <#cite_note-
    FOOTNOTEKeown201336-63> Buddhist traditions in Asia attempt to care
    for them on ritual-days every year, by leaving food and drinks in
    the open, to feed any hungry ghosts nearby.^[46] <#cite_note-
    FOOTNOTETrainor200462-52> When their bad karma demerit runs out,
    these beings are reborn into another realm. According to McClelland,
    this realm is the mildest of the three evil realms.^[57]
    <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcClelland2010114,_199-64> According to Yangsi
    Rinpoche, in contrast, the suffering of the beings born in the realm
    of the hungry ghosts is far more intense than those born in the
    animal realm.^[58] <#cite_note-65>
  * *Hell realm:*^[55] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrainor200463-62> beings in
    hell (Skt. /naraka/ <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
    Naraka_(Buddhism)>; P. /niraya/)^[47] <#cite_note-
    FOOTNOTEMcClelland2010136-53> enter this realm for evil karma such
    as theft, lying, adultery and others. The texts vary in their
    details, but typically describe numerous hellish regions each with
    different forms of intense suffering. These typically include eight
    hot hells and eight cold hells, as well as hells in which beings are
    eaten alive, beat, and tortured depending on the unwholesome karma
    accumulated.^[46] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrainor200462-52> Upon
    exhausting their unwholesome karma, the beings in hell perish and
    are born in successively higher realms.^[56] <#cite_note-
    FOOTNOTEKeown201336-63> This realm differs from the Christian
    conception of hell <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
    Hell_in_Christianity> in that existence in this realm is temporary
    and not final damnation.^[56] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeown201336-63> 

Tibetan Buddhism <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_Buddhism>
proposes that a buddha exists in each of the six realms. These six
buddhas have also been known as the "Six Sages." They are: Indraśakra
Buddha in the god realm, Vemacitra Buddha of the petty god realm,
Śākyamuni Buddha in the human realm; Sthīrasiṃha Buddha in the animal
realm, Jvālamukha Buddha in the hungry ghost realm, and Yāma Dharmarāja
as the buddha in the hot hell realm.^[59] <#cite_note-66>


Cause and end

[edit <https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?
title=Sa%E1%B9%83s%C4%81ra_(Buddhism)&action=edit&section=4>]

Samsara is perpetuated by one's karma, which is caused by craving and
ignorance <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avidy%C4%81_(Buddhism)> (/
avidyā/).^[20] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeown200481,_281-24> ^[21]
<#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowler199939–42-25> ^[note 5] <#cite_note-
Ignorance_and_craving-28>


Karma

[edit <https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?
title=Sa%E1%B9%83s%C4%81ra_(Buddhism)&action=edit&section=5>]
Main article: Karma in Buddhism <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Karma_in_Buddhism>

Samsara is perpetuated by karma.^[note 7] <#cite_note-70> Karma or
'action' results from an intentional physical or mental act, which
causes a future consequence.^[note 8] <#cite_note-72> Whether a deed is
wholesome or unwholesome is determined by whether its underlying
intention (cetanā <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cetan%C4%81>) is
wholesome or unwholesome.^[64] <#cite_note-73> Thus, one's present
existence in a particular realm and circumstance is determined by these
actions (i.e., /karma/) from one's previous lives; and the circumstances
of the future rebirth are determined by the actions in the current and
previous lives.^[note 9] <#cite_note-74>


Craving and ignorance

[edit <https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?
title=Sa%E1%B9%83s%C4%81ra_(Buddhism)&action=edit&section=6>]

Inconsistencies in the oldest texts show that the Buddhist teachings on
craving and ignorance, and the means to attain liberation, evolved,
either during the lifetime of the Buddha, or thereafter.^[65]
<#cite_note-75> According to Frauwallner, the Buddhist texts show a
shift in the explanation of the root cause of samsara.^[66]
<#cite_note-76> Originally craving was considered to be the root cause
of samsara,^[note 10] <#cite_note-80> which could be stilled by the
practice of /dhyāna <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Dhy%C4%81na_in_Buddhism>/, leading to a calm of mind which according to
Vetter /is/ the liberation which is being sought.^[70] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEVetter1988xxi-xxxvii-81> ^[71] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEBronkhorst199393-111-82>

The later Buddhist tradition considers ignorance <https://
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avidy%C4%81_(Buddhism)> to be the root cause of
samsara.^[67] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVetter1988xxi-77> ^[20] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEKeown200481,_281-24> ^[21] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFowler199939–
42-25> Avidya is misconception and ignorance about reality, leading to
grasping and clinging, and repeated rebirth.^[72] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEEdelglass20093-4-83> ^[73] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTELaumakis2008136-84> According to Paul Williams, "it is the not-
knowingness of things as they truly are, or of oneself as one really
is."^[74] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamsTribeWynne201246–47-85> It can be
overcome by insight into the true nature of reality. In the later
Buddhist tradition "liberating insight" came to be regarded as equally
liberating as the practice of /dhyana/.^[75] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEGombrich199799-102-86> ^[71] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEBronkhorst199393-111-82> According to Vetter and Bronkhorst,
this happened in response to other religious groups in India, who held
that a liberating insight was an indispensable requisite for /moksha
<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moksha>/, liberation from rebirth.^[76]
<#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVetter1988xxxii,_xxxiii-87> ^[77] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEBronkhorst199354-55,_96,_99-88> ^[note 11] <#cite_note-90>

The ideas on what exactly constituted this "liberating insight" evolved
over time.^[70] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVetter1988xxi-xxxvii-81> ^[79]
<#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBronkhorst1993chapter_7-91> Initially the term /
prajna <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praj%C3%B1%C4%81_(Buddhism)>/
served to denote this "liberating insight." Later on, /prajna/ was
replaced in the suttas by the four truths <https://en.wikipedia.org/
wiki/Four_Noble_Truths>.^[80] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEBronkhorst199399-100,_102-111-92> ^[81] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEAnderson1999-93> This happened in those texts where "liberating
insight" was preceded by the four jhanas, and where this practice of the
four jhanas then culminates in "liberating insight."^[82] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEBronkhorst1993108-94> ^[note 12] <#cite_note-97> The four truths
were superseded by /pratityasamutpada/, and still later, in the Hinayana
schools, by the doctrine of the non-existence of a substantial self or
person.^[85] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBronkhorst1993100-101-98> And
Schmithausen states that still other descriptions of this "liberating
insight" exist in the Buddhist canon:

    "that the five Skandhas are impermanent, disagreeable, and neither
    the Self nor belonging to oneself";^[note 13] <#cite_note-99> "the
    contemplation of the arising and disappearance (/udayabbaya/) of the
    five Skandhas";^[note 14] <#cite_note-100> "the realisation of the
    Skandhas as empty (/rittaka/), vain (/tucchaka/) and without any
    pith or substance (/asaraka/).^[note 15] <#cite_note-101> ^[86]
    <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBronkhorst1993101-102>


Liberation

[edit <https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?
title=Sa%E1%B9%83s%C4%81ra_(Buddhism)&action=edit&section=7>]
Main articles: Nirvana <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nirvana>,
Consciousness (Buddhism) <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Consciousness_(Buddhism)>, and Buddhist Paths to liberation <https://
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist_Paths_to_liberation>

Saṃsāra ends when one attains liberation (Skt. /mokṣa <https://
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moksha#Buddhism>/).^[87] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEWilliamsTribeWynne201230–42-103> ^[88] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEBuswellLopez2013304–305-104> ^[89] <#cite_note-105> ^[90]
<#cite_note-106> In early Buddhism, liberation is identified with
nirvana <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nirvana>. In later Buddhism,
liberation is tied to insight, especially the recognition and acceptance
of non-self.^[91] <#cite_note-107> Here, liberation from saṃsāra is
defined as no longer seeing any soul or self.^[9] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTERahula201451-58-10> ^[note 16] <#cite_note-109> This equating of
liberation and non-self appears throughout early Buddhist texts.^[93]
<#cite_note-110>

Some Buddhist texts suggest that rebirth occurs through the transfer of
consciousness (Skt. /vijiñāna/; P. /vinnana <https://en.wikipedia.org/
wiki/Consciousness_(Buddhism)>/) from one life to another. When this
consciousness ceases, then liberation is attained.^[94] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEWaldron200322-111> There is a connection between consciousness,
karmic activities, and the cycle of rebirth in that, with the
destruction of consciousness, there is "destruction and cessation of
"karmic activities" (anabhisankhara, S III, 53), which are considered in
Buddhism to be "necessary for the continued perpetuation of cyclic
existence."^[94] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaldron200322-111>

While Buddhism considers the liberation from samsara as the ultimate
spiritual goal, in traditional practice, Buddhists seek and accumulate
merit through good deeds, donations to monks and various Buddhist
rituals in order to gain better rebirths rather than nirvana.^[95]
<#cite_note-112>


Impermanence and Non-Self Reality

[edit <https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?
title=Sa%E1%B9%83s%C4%81ra_(Buddhism)&action=edit&section=8>]
Main articles: Impermanence <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Impermanence>, Anitya <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anitya>, and Anicca
<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anicca>

A value of Buddhism is the idea of impermanence <https://
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impermanence>. All living things, causes,
conditions, situations are impermanent.^[96] <#cite_note-113>
Impermanence is the idea that all things disappear once they have
originated. Impermanence <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impermanence>
occurs "moment to moment",^[97] <#cite_note-114> and this is why there
is no recognition of the self.^[98] <#cite_note-115> Since everything is
in a state of decay, permanent happiness and self cannot exist in
samsara.^[99] <#cite_note-116>

Anatta <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatta> is the Buddhist idea of
non-self. Winston L. King, a writer from the University of Hawai'i
Press, references two integral parts of Anatta in /Philosophy East and
West./^[100] <#cite_note-117> King details the first aspect, that Anatta
<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatta> can be "experienced and not just
described."^[101] <#cite_note-118> King states the second aspect of
Anatta <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatta> is that it is the
liberation from the "power of samsaric drives."^[102] <#cite_note-119>
Obtaining awareness of Anatta <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatta> and
non-self reality results in a, "freedom from the push-pull of his own
appetites, passions, ambitions, and fixations and from the external
world's domination in general, that is, the conquest of greed, hatred,
and delusion."^[103] <#cite_note-120> This "push-pull" of mundane human
existence or samsara results in dukka <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Dukkha>, but the recognition of Anatta <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Anatta> results in a "freedom from the push-pull."


Psychological interpretation

[edit <https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?
title=Sa%E1%B9%83s%C4%81ra_(Buddhism)&action=edit&section=9>]

According to Chögyam Trungpa <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/
Ch%C3%B6gyam_Trungpa> the realms of samsara can refer to both
"psychological states of mind and physical cosmological realms".^[note
17] <#cite_note-122>

Gethin argues, rebirth in the different realms is determined by one's
karma <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karma_in_Buddhism>, which is
directly determined by one's psychological states. The Buddhist
cosmology may thus be seen as a map of different realms of existence and
a description of all possible psychological experiences.^[105]
<#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGethin1998119–120-123> The psychological states of a
person in current life lead to the nature of next rebirth in Buddhist
cosmology.^[106] <#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGethin1998121-124>

Paul Williams acknowledges Gethin's suggestion of the "principle of the
equivalence of cosmology and psychology," but notes that Gethin is not
asserting the Buddhist cosmology is really all about current or
potential states of mind or psychology.^[107] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEWilliams200278–79-125> The realms in Buddhist cosmology are
indeed realms of rebirths. Otherwise rebirth would always be into the
human realm, or there would be no rebirth at all. And that is not
traditional Buddhism, states Williams.^[107] <#cite_note-
FOOTNOTEWilliams200278–79-125>

David McMahan concludes that the attempts to construe ancient Buddhist
cosmology in modern psychological terms is modernistic reconstruction,
"detraditionalization and demythologization" of Buddhism, a sociological
phenomenon that is seen in all religions.^[108] <#cite_note-126>

A pre-modern form of this interpretation can be seen in the views of the
sixth-century Chinese monk Zhiyi <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhiyi>,
whose writings became the foundation for the Tiantai <https://
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiantai> school in China, particularly in a
concept named "the trichiliocosm in a single instant of thought" (一念三
千 Ch. /yíniàn sānqiān/; Ja. /ichinen sanzen/), which proposes that the
vastness of all space is contained in the shortest span of a single
thought.^[109] <#cite_note-127> The /Record of Linji/, an anthology of
the teachings of the ninth-century Chinese monk Linji Yixuan <https://
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linji_Yixuan>, also presents the view that the
Three Realms <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_realms> originate with
the mind.
